opus-5.5.text:
Next-token prediction is often underestimated and often overestimated, and both mistakes come from the same confusion. The objective is very simple, but what you have to learn to minimize it on a huge, diverse corpus is not simple at all. If you want to predict the next line of a proof or the next step of a derivation, you have to model whatever produced that text. To some degree that means modeling the reasoning itself. So I don't think it's fair to dismiss these systems as just autocomplete. The training signal is remarkably rich.

That said, I don't think next-token prediction by itself is a sufficient foundation for reliable reasoning. The core issue is verification. A model trained purely to imitate text learns what plausible reasoning looks like. It doesn't necessarily learn whether a given chain of reasoning is correct. In mathematics, which is where I've spent most of my time thinking about this, plausible and correct can be very far apart. A proof that is 99% right is wrong. With autoregressive generation, errors compound. One subtly wrong step early on and everything after it is built on sand, and the model has no intrinsic mechanism to notice.

So my view has long been that you need to close the loop. You want the model to generate, but you also want something that checks, ideally something formal. That's why I've been so interested in autoformalization: translating natural-language mathematics into formal systems where a proof checker can verify every step. Once you have a verifier, next-token prediction stops being the whole story and becomes a proposal mechanism. The model proposes, the verifier disposes, and you can do search and reinforcement learning on top of that. You're no longer limited by the quality of human-written data. You can bootstrap beyond it, the way AlphaZero went beyond human games, because you have a ground-truth signal.

I'd frame it this way. Next-token prediction is an excellent way to acquire a prior, a kind of intuition about which steps are promising. Reasoning in the strong sense needs that intuition plus grounding and search. Humans work similarly. A good mathematician has strong intuition about what's likely true, but they don't trust it until they've checked it. The systems that will reason really well are the ones that combine the generative power we already have with rigorous verification. I'm quite optimistic about that combination. I think it's the path to systems that can do mathematics at a superhuman level, and from there reasoning more broadly.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think next-token prediction gets underestimated by a lot of people, and I understand why. On the surface it sounds trivial, right? You're just guessing the next word. But if you take it seriously, predicting the next token well on the kind of data we have means you have to model the process that generated that data. And that process includes people reasoning, making arguments, correcting their mistakes, deriving things step by step. So the objective itself is not the limitation. In the limit, a perfect next-token predictor on a sufficiently rich corpus would have to internalize a lot of the actual structure of reasoning.

Where I'm more skeptical is whether the training signal gets you there efficiently. Most text is not a faithful trace of how people think. It's the polished output. The false starts, the backtracking, the verification, all of that is mostly missing from the data. So the model sees conclusions far more often than it sees the search that produced them. That's why I've always been drawn to formal domains, mathematics in particular, because there you can actually generate the search process, you can verify it, and you get a signal that tells you whether the reasoning was correct and not just whether it sounded plausible.

The other thing I'd say is that reasoning, at least the kind I care about, is fundamentally about search and verification. Next-token prediction gives you a very good prior over what a reasonable next step might be. That's enormously valuable, it's what makes the search tractable at all. But a prior is not a proof. You still need something on top, some mechanism that explores, checks, and feeds the result back. So my view is that next-token prediction is a very strong foundation, maybe the strongest one we've found, but it's the foundation and not the whole building. The interesting work is in how you close the loop between generation and verification, and how you make that loop produce its own training data, because that's where you stop being bounded by what humans happened to write down.

astra-6.text:
I think next-token prediction is a very powerful learning objective, but we should distinguish between producing a plausible continuation and producing a correct argument. They can overlap—a model can learn useful reasoning patterns from predicting text—but the objective itself doesn’t guarantee correctness.

For me, mathematics is an especially interesting setting because you can make that distinction precise. A model can propose a proof, and a formal proof checker can tell you whether it is valid. Then you can combine the model’s ability to suggest promising steps with search and verification.

So I wouldn’t dismiss next-token prediction. I would ask what we build around it. Can the system explore alternatives, recognize when a step fails, and use reliable feedback to improve? That seems more important than whether its individual proposals are generated one token at a time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think next-token prediction is a very powerful learning signal, but I would distinguish between learning to produce plausible reasoning and learning to reason reliably. To predict text well, a model has to capture quite a lot of structure about the world. So I wouldn’t dismiss it as merely a statistical trick.

The question is what happens when you go beyond problems that resemble the training distribution. A sequence of steps can look convincing while containing a small error that invalidates everything that follows. And the prediction objective itself doesn’t give you a guarantee that those steps are correct.

That’s why I’m particularly interested in mathematics and formal reasoning. You can have a model propose a proof, and then a formal system checks whether it is valid. That gives you a much stronger feedback signal than whether the answer sounds right. Next-token prediction can be a very useful component of that system, but I don’t think we should assume that scaling that objective alone resolves the problem of reliable reasoning.
